catalog_quote: The basic rule is to count back two vowels from the end and place an accent on that vowel. In counting back those two vowels, skip any epenthetic vowels (an -e- inserted to break up an unallowed cluster of consonants) in final syllables or stem joiners (an -a- that connects a noun root to a verb root in a complex stem). The next step is to test for certain special conditions that may alter the accent. 1. If the accented vowel is immediately before a glottal stop then the glottal stop is dropped and the vowel is lengthened and given a falling tone ... 2. If the accented vowel is immediately before an -hl-, -hy-, -hw-, or -hn-, then the -h- is dropped and the vowel is lengthened and given a falling tone ... 3. sweep_summary: Oneida (onei1249, catalog 'weight': penult accent, shifting to the ultima after a lengthened open penult; deciding source Abbott 2006 Teaching Grammar pp. 47-48, held). this search of works with stress in the title's four title-hits are three records of one work in two forms, Michelson's 1983 Harvard dissertation (two Glottolog records) and its 1988 Kluwer revision A Comparative Study of Lake-Iroquoian Accent (ch. 3 'Accent' pp. 52-120, Oneida pp. 66-71), plus one Glottolog mis-attachment (Klerke et al. 2015, an NLP paper on MT reading metrics; not relevant). None of the Michelson texts could be opened: Springer PDF redirects to a login, link.springer.com serves a client challenge, archive. Harvard holds the 1988 book in print (Widener PM1382.M5 1988). Michelson 1988 ch. 3 remains the high-priority acquisition because it alone settles whether the shifting 'accent' is the stress the catalog codes (our 'weight') or a pitch accent over fixed penult stress (StressTyp2/WALS 'penultimate'). One new open source was found and read: the Stanford Phonology Archive (Crothers et al. 1979) Oneida entry (archive.org one_SPA1979_phon, saved with page image), which carries Lounsbury 1953's accent statement verbatim (one culminative accent per word; pitch peak on final short vowels, loudness+pitch elsewhere; penult accent historical; position needs morphological knowledge). It refines but does not change the catalog's classification and does not supersede Abbott. Also flagged: the Michelson & Doxtator 2002 dictionary sentence banked by the earlier search came from a vdoc.pub/a site we do not cite and should not be treated as a read page.org, Crossref, PMC and direct downloads.

new_statements.reading: Lounsbury (1953), as carried verbatim by the Stanford Phonology Archive, describes Oneida as having one culminative word accent per inflected word (utterance-medially), realised as a pitch peak alone when it falls on a word-final short vowel and as loudness plus pitch elsewhere; penultimate accent is reconstructed for an earlier stage, and the synchronic position is not phonemically predictable without knowing the morphemes. This is compatible with the catalog's surface pattern (penult accent, or ultima accent after a lengthened open penult, with counting that skips epenthetic vowels and joiner vowels) and with the fact that final-vowel accents are realised by pitch, but it states neither the weight rule nor Michelson's stress/accent distinction; it neither confirms nor contradicts the 'weight' coding, it refines the record with the oldest first-hand description and the phonetic realisation. It is a quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2 (SPA quoting Lounsbury), not a page of Lounsbury.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Every inflected word (utterance-medially) carries exactly one accent, on one of its last five syllables; it is realised as a pitch peak on word-final short vowels and as loudness plus pitch elsewhere. Historically the accent was mechanically penultimate; synchronically Lounsbury says its position is not predictable from the phonemic string alone but needs morphological information (which vowels are epenthetic etc.). In the text analyses he states the surface alternation: accent moves from the penult to the final syllable when only one consonant separates the two vowels, with lengthening of the (now pretonic) penult when the final vowel is followed by a consonant or length; vowel length otherwise occurs after the accented vowel.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned in the snippets ('one and only one accent' per word).
new_statements.exceptions: Forms 'too short for the morphophonemics of accent placement' are indexed in the morpheme tables (p. 38 fn.): they 'either carry the accent in a word or carry the pretonic length before a single consonant'; utterance-final forms undergo final unvoicing (3.3, pp. 33-34), where the accent on final short vowels is a pitch peak only.
new_statements.identity_note: Lounsbury 1953 describes Oneida as spoken in Wisconsin (fieldwork for the WPA Oneida Language and Folklore Project, Oneida, Wisconsin, 1939-40); the catalog's Abbott 2006 is also Wisconsin Oneida; Michelson's works describe the Ontario (Thames) dialect.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Accent /'/ is a phoneme of Oneida (p. 27). Every word in utterance-medial position carries exactly one accent, located somewhere in the last five syllables; historically it was a mechanical penultimate accent, but synchronically its position cannot be predicted from the phonemic shape of the word alone and requires knowing the morphemes (p. 33; morphemes are indexed in the lists for whether they 'carry the accent in a word or carry the pretonic length before a single consonant', p. 38 fn.). Phonetically the accent is a pitch peak alone when it falls on a word-final (phrase-medial) short vowel, and a peak of loudness plus pitch elsewhere (Table 1, p. 30); accented long vowels have a falling contour, unaccented long vowels a level contour (p. 30). Vowel length occurs after an accented vowel and/or after the vowel of the pretonic syllable of some words (p. 32). In the text notes he states the productive alternation behind the surface pattern: the accent shifts from the penult to the final syllable when only a single consonant separates the two vowels, with concomitant lengthening of the penultimate vowel when the final vowel is followed by a consonant or by length (p. 96); in an accented syllable glottal stop is replaced by vowel length with falling tone (pp. 86, 96).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None: 'one and only one accent' per utterance-medial word (p. 33). Pretonic vowel length (p. 32, p. 38 fn.) is described as length, not as a secondary accent.
new_statements.exceptions: Accent window = last five syllables (p. 33); penult-to-final shift across a single intervening consonant with penult lengthening (p. 96); forms 'too short for the morphophonemics of accent placement' are specially indexed (p. 38 fn.); utterance-final forms undergo final unvoicing and other phonemic alteration, so citations are given in utterance-medial (phrase-medial) shape (pp. 31, 33-34); word-final accented short vowels realised by pitch only (p. 30); younger speakers simplify /wy/ to /y/ (p. 32, segmental only).
new_statements.identity_note: Lounsbury's material comes from the Oneida Language and Folklore Project (referred to as 'the Project' on p. 93), i.e. Oneida as spoken in Wisconsin c. 1939-40; the snippets read do not name the community explicitly, so the Wisconsin attribution rests on the work's known provenance rather than on a page seen here. He notes generational variation only for a segmental cluster (/wy/ > /y/ among younger speakers, p. 32).

readall_conflicts: No disagreement on placement. Lounsbury 1953 (p. 33) frames Oneida accent as phonemic and not predictable from phonemic shape without morphemic knowledge, one accent per word within the last five syllables, historically penultimate; the catalog (Abbott, coded 'weight') and Michelson-type analyses state a penult-based rule that skips epenthetic and joiner vowels and shifts to the ultima across a single consonant. Lounsbury himself states that shift (p. 96) and the historical penult, so the sources describe the same surface facts; the difference is analytic (lexical/morphological indexing in a 1953 phonemic description vs. a rule over morphologically annotated vowels), and the catalog's 'weight' label is neither confirmed nor denied by his wording.
